0.body: A lean viewer for Phoebus Display Builder .bob screens, written in Rust with egui . It also opens the older CS-Studio BOY .opi screens. It shows live EPICS Channel Access and PV Access values, including areaDetector images, and is small enough to run on a phone, in the Android 16 Linux Terminal (Debian 13, aarch64). The same app runs in a browser, served by bobview-server. Scripts (Jython/JavaScript), display editing, alarm and archiver services are out of scope; see Scope and fidelity to Phoebus . Learning: acquiring skills Working: applying skills Practical: doing Theoretical: knowing 📚 Tutorials learning-oriented New to bobview? Install it, start the simulated beamline and open your first live display. 🧭 How-to guides goal-oriented Practical steps: connect to real IOCs, run over ssh, open BOY screens, save layouts, deploy the web server. 💡 Explanations understanding-oriented Background and design: what bobview aims to do, how it is built, how its windows and writes behave. 📖 Reference information-oriented Command-line options, supported widgets, macros and rules, browser parameters and the Rust API. The Rust API docs for the workspace's crates are published alongside this book. The docs follow the Diátaxis framework: four kinds of page for four needs, learning, doing, understanding and looking things up.
0.title: bobview

1.body: This tutorial installs bobview, starts a simulated beamline on your own machine and walks you around its displays. It takes about ten minutes and needs no EPICS installation and no IOCs: bobview-testioc plays the part of the epics-containers example-services BL01T beamline. You need an x86_64 or aarch64 Linux machine (an Android phone's Linux Terminal works), or a Mac.

111.body: $(X) and ${X}, with defaults. Widget properties such as $(pv_name), and $(actions) in a tooltip. Macros pass down through groups, tabs and embedded displays. In displays opened from files, a macro that isn't defined falls back to the environment variable of the same name (in widget properties and the display name). The display name, with macros expanded (or the file name if it has none), is the window title. Give macros on the command line with -m P=X,R=Y, or in a browser with &macros=P=X,R=Y.

112.body: Rules are expressions over pv0, pvStr0, pvSev0, pvLegacySev0 … that set any property, or one item of a list such as symbols[0], including the position, size and PV. Output expression rules are supported, and macros in rules are expanded. Operators: arithmetic, bitwise (including shifts) and logical. Operators bind as in Phoebus's Jython for a .bob, or BOY's JavaScript for an .opi. A lone = is == in a .bob, as Phoebus makes it. Unlike Jython, bitwise operators take the integer part of a double such as pv0, where Jython fails the rule. In an .opi, pvSev0 becomes pvLegacySev0 (BOY's severity numbers) and widget.getValue() reads the widget's own PV.

120.body: The navigator button shows, beside the main window's display, a tree of the displays the home display links to, the displays those link to, and so on. A display's links are its widgets' Open display actions, including those in groups, tabs and embedded displays, each display and macros once, named by its button's text (or, in a menu, the action's description). A link with no text of its own, or the same text as another link on its display (a row of identical device symbols), is named by the display it opens once that has been read: by the words of its title that macros fill in, such as LB-VA-IONP-04 from Ion Pump Controller - $(device), else by its whole title. The tooltip gives the title, file and macros. Clicking a node opens its display as a link in the main window would, so with the main window pinned it goes to the viewer; shift and ctrl work as for a link. Displays open in a window are in bold . Displays are read from their files, without connecting their PVs, as their nodes are shown, so the tree is read one level ahead of what is open. A display that links back to one above it is marked ↻ and not opened again; one that can't be read is marked ⚠. A command action's display (a DLS launcher script) is found by running its script, so only when its node is opened or clicked. The filter box lists the displays read so far whose name or file matches; ⟳ reads them all again. Showing or hiding the navigator widens or narrows the window by its width (unless maximised or full screen), so the display keeps its size and zoom.

125.body: A pure-Rust EPICS IOC that serves, over Channel Access and PV Access, a subset of the PVs of the epics-containers example-services BL01T beamline, enough for its opi/demo.bob screen. It has no C dependencies, so it runs natively on an aarch64 phone where the real amd64 IOC containers would need qemu. Built on the epics-rs crates; uses about 15 MB RSS while streaming images. bobview-testioc [--only ea|motor|cam]... # default: all three It needs no shell and keeps running with stdin closed. --only applies to both protocols. Its environment variables are in Environment variables .
125.title: bobview-testioc

126.body: part PVs how ea bl01t:A, bl01t:B, bl01t:SUM bl01t-ea-test-01's ioc.db verbatim, A=2.54, B=2.61 motor BL01T-MO-SIMC-01:M1, :M2 real motor record (motor-rs) on a simulated axis cam BL01T-DI-CAM-01:DET:, :ARR:, :PVA: soft records plus a small driver loop The camera is not a real simDetector: it serves the ADBase / NDPluginBase records the demo screen uses (Acquire, AcquireTime, AcquirePeriod, ArrayCounter, ImageMode, NumImages, DetectorState_RBV, FilePath, ...) and counts frames at the acquire period, honouring Single / Multiple / Continuous. As in its ioc.yaml it starts acquiring continuously at AcquireTime 0.1.
126.title: PVs

127.body: Every record is also served over PVA the way QSRV does it: NTScalar for analog and long records (with display, control and alarm metadata), NTEnum for bi / bo / mbbi / mbbo, NTScalarArray for waveforms; gets, puts and monitors all work. BL01T-DI-CAM-01:PVA:OUTPUT is an NTNDArray like NDPluginPVA's output. The image is simulated: 1024x1024 Int8 (byteValue, pixels 0..255 stored as i8 bit patterns, as an Int8 simDetector produces), uncompressed, with drifting diagonal fringes, three gaussian spots on Lissajous paths and some noise. A frame is posted for every frame counted (10 Hz by default) while DET:ArrayCallbacks and PVA:EnableCallbacks are both on; uniqueId is the frame counter. To look at a frame without a viewer: cargo run -p testioc --example frame_png -- /tmp/frame 1 50
127.title: PV Access

128.body: From x86_64: cargo zigbuild --release --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu.2.36 -p testioc

129.body: The workspace's crates are documented with rustdoc, built into this book under api/. Libraries: bob : the display model, .bob and .opi reading, macros and project links pv : PV connections over CA, PVA, PVWS and local sources testioc : the test IOC Programs, documented with their private items, since that is all they have: bobview : the viewer, its egui app and widgets bobview_server : the web server and its PV Web Socket bobview_probe and bobview_testioc : the command-line front ends of bobview-probe and bobview-testioc The crates are not published to crates.io and their API is not stable; it is documented for contributors. In a local build the links work when the book is built with scripts/build-docs.sh (see Build from source ), not with a plain mdbook serve.

130.body: bobview is Apache-2.0. The release binaries include third-party crates, among them the epics-rs CA and PVA libraries (EPICS-style open licence), and embed the Liberation Sans fonts and a symbol subset of Noto Sans Math (both SIL Open Font Licence) and egui's default fonts. A display can be a file or an http:// / https:// URL, on the command line or typed into Open… : bobview http://host:8080/opi/demo.bob Files that a display names (buttons, embedded displays, navigation tabs) are found relative to it, so a directory of screens served by any web server works as it does from disk. 28.body: bobview draws with OpenGL. Two commands start it: command draws with use it bobview the machine's own OpenGL: the GPU, or whatever driver the desktop provides normally: on a local desktop, a laptop, a Mac, the phone bobview-ssh Mesa in software, on the CPU of the machine bobview runs on when the OpenGL path can't work, such as over ssh -X Both take the same arguments. Start with bobview, and switch to bobview-ssh if it fails to start or draws nothing.

29.body: Over ssh -X or -Y. This is what it was named for. Forwarded OpenGL reaches your local X server as indirect GLX, which current X servers refuse, so bobview exits with glutin error: [2] BadValue. Where a GPU driver is installed but can't be used , for example a remote desktop, VNC or Xvfb session on a machine with an NVIDIA driver: glvnd picks NVIDIA's GL, which then has no GPU display to draw on. Where the GPU driver is broken or misbehaves, as a workaround while you sort it out. There is no need for it on macOS, on Wayland or X11 desktops with working graphics, in the Android Linux Terminal, or for --snapshot, unless one of the cases above applies.

30.body: bobview-ssh is a small script that runs bobview with: LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1, so Mesa renders on the CPU (llvmpipe); __GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME=mesa, and __EGL_VENDOR_LIBRARY_FILENAMES pointing at Mesa's EGL vendor file, so libglvnd picks Mesa rather than a GPU vendor's library such as NVIDIA's. Over X forwarding the finished window then travels to your X server as plain images, which every X server accepts. Software rendering costs CPU on the machine running bobview, but bobview's displays are simple to draw, so it is usually quick enough. Over ssh -X each redraw sends the whole window over the network, so bobview redraws a window only for its own input and when a PV it shows changes, at most 10 times a second (see Pinned windows and the viewer ).

31.body: Mesa must be installed where bobview runs: mesa-dri-drivers on RHEL, libgl1-mesa-dri on Debian and Ubuntu (both are in the install prerequisites ).
31.title: Requirement

32.body:
ssh -X control-host
bobview-ssh /path/to/screen.bob -m P=BL01T Layouts restore window positions over X forwarding; see Save and restore a layout .

33.body: Any .opi file opens like a .bob: bobview screen.opi BOY screens often name each other through the CS-Studio workspace, though: an Eclipse project whose .project links folder names (mks937a, dlsPLC …) to the directories that hold each module's screens, so ../mks937a/gauge.opi means the mks937a link. This page shows how to open such screens so that their links work. How BOY screens are translated explains the rules behind it.
33.breadcrumbs: Open BOY screens from an Eclipse project or DLS module » Open BOY screens from an Eclipse project or DLS module
33.title: Open BOY screens from an Eclipse project or DLS module

34.body: Open the screen through its project path: bobview /workspaces/VacOPIS/vacuum_4-100/vacuum/diamondVacuumOverview.opi for a project in /workspaces/VacOPIS/vacuum_4-100. bobview follows the project's links (the linked folders need not exist on disk; Open… lists them). Or give the screen's real path and name the project with --project: bobview -p /workspaces/VacOPIS/vacuum_4-100 /dls_sw/…/vacuumApp/opi/opi/diamondVacuumOverview.opi
34.breadcrumbs: Open BOY screens from an Eclipse project or DLS module » Through an Eclipse project
34.title: Through an Eclipse project

35.body: DLS modules need neither. There is no .project on disk, but the generated launcher runcss.sh beside a module's screens (vacuumApp/opi/opi) lists the links it gives CS-Studio. bobview reads that list (it does not run the script), so just open the screen by its real path: bobview /dls_sw/…/vacuum/4-100/vacuumApp/opi/opi/diamondVacuumOverview.opi This works for a BOY screen reached by its real path from anywhere (the file chooser, a layout, an absolute path in another screen), with the launcher in its folder or up to two above. To open another module's BOY screen through this module's links, give -p the module's screens folder (or its runcss.sh).
35.breadcrumbs: Open BOY screens from an Eclipse project or DLS module » A DLS module
35.title: A DLS module

36.body: DLS screens are often opened by a launcher script, such as ./srCellVacuum 04, that supplies macros. For an .opi given on the command line in an Eclipse project (through its project path or with --project), bobview tries the launcher scripts in its directory to find them: the one named <screen>.sh first, with no arguments and with each number in the file name, bare and with an r. So: screen macros from linacVacuum.opi linacVacuum.sh (dom=LI) srCell05Vacuum.opi srCellVacuum 05 SR05C_rack.opi srCellVacuum 05r Macros given with -m override these. Screens with no number in their name (srInjCellVacuum.opi is cell 01) need -m with the macros their launcher would give, or opening from the overview.
36.breadcrumbs: Open BOY screens from an Eclipse project or DLS module » A screen that needs launcher macros
36.title: A screen that needs launcher macros

37.body: A layout records the open windows so that a control-room arrangement can be put back with one command. Pinned windows and the viewer explains how windows are opened in the first place.
37.breadcrumbs: Save and restore a layout » Save and restore a layout
37.title: Save and restore a layout

38.body: Arrange the windows, then use the main toolbar's ☰ menu: Save layout as… names a new layout (asking before replacing one). Save layout saves to the layout last loaded or saved. Save as default makes it the layout bobview starts with. Save default on exit (off unless ticked) saves the default each time you quit. Delete layout removes one.
38.breadcrumbs: Save and restore a layout » Save
38.title: Save

39.body:
Pick a layout from the toolbar's layout list; this closes the display and trend windows open now. From the command line: bobview # restores the default layout if there is one
bobview DISPLAY # opens DISPLAY; the default layout is not restored
bobview --layout rf-shift # restores layouts/rf-shift.json
bobview --no-layout # ignores the default layout --snapshot ignores layouts.
39.breadcrumbs: Save and restore a layout » Restore
39.title: Restore

4.body: Tell the Channel Access client to look for PVs on this machine, and start the viewer: EPICS_CA_ADDR_LIST=127.0.0.1 bobview With no display named, bobview opens index.bob from the test screens it installed. You should see live values within a second or two.
4.title: 3. Open the displays

40.body: For each window: its display, Eclipse project and effective macros, its position and size, whether it is pinned, and whether a display window shows its toolbar; for the main window also its zoom and whether it shows the navigator. For each trend window: its PVs, time span, log scale, position and size. A layout from before windows were pinned pins them all if it was saved in multi-window mode, and none if not. Layouts are JSON files in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/bobview/layouts (by default ~/.config/bobview/layouts), so they can be copied between machines or kept under version control.
40.breadcrumbs: Save and restore a layout » What a layout holds
40.title: What a layout holds

41.body: A saved position that is on none of the monitors now (a laptop that was docked) is dropped and the window manager places the window. Wayland does not let an application read or set its windows' positions, so on a Wayland desktop a layout restores the windows and their sizes but the compositor places them, and bobview logs this once. To keep positions, run bobview under XWayland: WAYLAND_DISPLAY= bobview X11 desktops, including bobview-ssh over X forwarding, restore positions.
41.breadcrumbs: Save and restore a layout » Positions on Wayland and with changed monitors
41.title: Positions on Wayland and with changed monitors

42.body: A trend window plots one or more PVs against time.
42.title: Trend PVs

43.body: Right-click a widget (long-press on a touch screen) and pick Trend for its PV, or Trend with rule PVs for its PV and the PVs its rules read. In a BOY screen, a button that would open a Data Browser or StripTool opens a trend of its PVs instead (see How BOY screens are translated ). Several trends may be open at once, each in its own window over the display, and they stay open as you move between displays. Layouts save them.
43.title: Open a trend

44.body: Pick the time span from the window's menu: 1 minute to 1 day (10 minutes by default). The value axis fits the data. Switch Log scale on for a value axis on a log scale. The legend below the plot gives each PV's colour, name and current value, or Disconnected. ✖ removes a PV, and Add PV adds one.
44.title: Use a trend

45.body: A trend is live only: each PV gets a sample on every update from when the window opened (up to 100 000 samples, and a day, per PV), with no archived history. Each value holds until the next, and a gap marks where a PV was disconnected.
45.title: Limits

46.body: Serve displays to a browser runs bobview-server for this machine only. This guide makes it reachable from others, safely. All of its options are in Command line .
46.breadcrumbs: Deploy bobview-server for others » Deploy bobview-server for others
46.title: Deploy bobview-server for others

47.body: The server reaches PVs through bobview's own CA/PVA client, so run it anywhere caget works, with the usual EPICS_* variables: bobview-server --opi /path/to/displays --bind 0.0.0.0 The release tarball includes the web build, which the server finds in share/bobview/web. Files in --opi take precedence over files of the same name in the web build (which has the test displays).
47.breadcrumbs: Deploy bobview-server for others » Run it where PVs are reachable
47.title: Run it where PVs are reachable

48.body: By default it listens on --bind 127.0.0.1 --port 8080. Use --bind 0.0.0.0 (every interface) or a specific address to serve others, ideally behind a firewall or an authenticating reverse proxy, since reading PVs needs no login. Browsers let any page open a websocket, so the server accepts only pages from itself (by Origin), plus any you name: bobview-server --opi DIR --bind 0.0.0.0 --allow-origin https://ops.example.com Those pages must also call the server by an IP address, localhost, this machine's name (as the kernel has it, without its domain, or in a domain of /etc/resolv.conf), the host of an --allow-origin, or a name given with --host NAME (repeatable), so that a page cannot reach it through a DNS name of its own.
48.breadcrumbs: Deploy bobview-server for others » Choose who can reach it
48.title: Choose who can reach it

49.body: Give the public name the proxy passes on as Host with --host NAME. Every client has the proxy's address, so raise --max-per-ip (default 10) and expect the logs to show the proxy.
49.breadcrumbs: Deploy bobview-server for others » Behind a reverse proxy
49.title: Behind a reverse proxy

5.body: Hover over a widget: a tooltip shows its PV and value. Right-click a widget (long-press on a touch screen): copy the PV name or value, open the PV's details, or Trend it. A trend window plots the PV against time; leave it open. Click a button that opens another display. Use Back and Forward in the toolbar to move between them, and Home to return to index.bob. Click the zoom in the toolbar to see the display at 100%, then Fit to fit it to the window again. On a touch screen, pinch to zoom. Open the navigator from the toolbar to see a tree of every display reachable from the home display.
5.title: 4. Look around

50.body: Writes are off unless the server has --write, since they go out as the server's user. Each write must then carry a token. Set it in the environment rather than with --write-token, since arguments show in ps: BOBVIEW_WRITE_TOKEN=s3cret bobview-server --opi DIR --write With neither, the server makes a random token and prints it to stderr at startup; an empty BOBVIEW_WRITE_TOKEN counts as unset. Users open the page with &token=TOKEN. See Writes and safety for how the token is protected.
50.breadcrumbs: Deploy bobview-server for others » Allow writes
50.title: Allow writes

51.body: At most 100 clients and 50,000 subscribed PVs. At most 10 clients from one address (or one IPv6 /64), --max-per-ip N. A client subscribing to more than 1,000 new PVs a second, after its first 10,000, is slowed down. A client that stops answering websocket pings, or takes over 10 s to take one message, is dropped. PV names over 256 characters, or with spaces or non-ASCII characters, are refused. Each client gets the PVs that changed at most every --throttle-ms (100 ms), each with its latest state. It serves no loc:// or sim:// PVs: the page makes those itself. Images from PVA are not sent over PVWS yet.
51.breadcrumbs: Deploy bobview-server for others » Limits it enforces
51.title: Limits it enforces

52.body: Dot-files such as .git are never served, nor files reached through a symbolic link that leads out of --opi or --web (unless --follow-symlinks). Other sites cannot frame the pages (X-Frame-Options, frame-ancestors 'self').
52.breadcrumbs: Deploy bobview-server for others » Files it will not serve
52.title: Files it will not serve

53.body: --snapshot renders a display to a PNG without opening a window, then exits. It is useful for documentation, regression checks and CI. bobview --snapshot out.png screen.bob
53.title: Take snapshots

54.body:
bobview --snapshot out.png --size 1920x1080 screen.bob
bobview --snapshot out.png --size auto screen.bob # as a window manager would size it
bobview --snapshot phone.png --scale-factor 2.75 screen.bob # as on a high-DPI phone --size defaults to 1280x800. auto starts at the window's default size and resizes it as a window manager would, on a monitor of 1920x1080 points.
54.title: Size and scale

55.body: PVs get 2 seconds to connect by default; give more with --wait: bobview --snapshot out.png --wait 5 screen.bob
55.title: Wait for PVs

56.body: --click X,Y and --right-click X,Y (repeatable, in the order given) interact with the display before the snapshot, which is taken --settle seconds (default 1) after the last click. Positions are in pixels. bobview --snapshot menu.png --right-click 200,150 --settle 0.5 screen.bob
56.title: Click first

57.body:
CI does this against bobview-testioc: bobview-testioc &
export EPICS_CA_ADDR_LIST=127.0.0.1 EPICS_CA_AUTO_ADDR_LIST=NO
for f in tests/displays/*.bob; do bobview --snapshot "snapshots/$(basename "$f" .bob).png" --size 1280x800 --wait 5 "$f"
done
kill %1

The docs are an mdBook : cargo install mdbook
scripts/build-docs.sh serve --open This builds the Rust API docs into the book under api/, then serves it; mdbook serve rebuilds and reloads the page as you edit. Run it again to pick up changes to the API docs. scripts/build-docs.sh alone builds the book into docs/book.

63.body: The Docs workflow builds the book and the API docs on every pull request. On a push to main or a v* tag it publishes them to the gh-pages branch in a folder named after the branch or tag, writes switcher.json (the list of versions for the menu in the top bar) and leaves the other versions in place. The site's root redirects to main/.
63.breadcrumbs: Build from source » How the docs are published
63.title: How the docs are published

64.body:
Push a tag such as v0.2.2: git tag v0.2.2
git push origin v0.2.2 CI creates the GitHub Release itself and builds with the version taken from the tag, so Cargo.toml needs no bump. It builds on native runners for each platform (ubuntu-24.04, ubuntu-24.04-arm and macOS) and attaches a bobview-<arch>-<os>.tar.gz for each, such as bobview-x86_64-linux.tar.gz and bobview-aarch64-linux.tar.gz. The Linux builds use cargo zigbuild to link against glibc 2.28, so they run on RHEL 8+, Ubuntu 20.04+ and Debian 10+. Each tarball carries THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt, generated by scripts/third-party-licenses.py. install.sh downloads the latest release for the machine it runs on. The tag also publishes a copy of these docs at https://gilesknap.github.io/bobview/<tag>/, which the version menu in the docs' top bar then lists beside main.
64.breadcrumbs: Make a release » Make a release
64.title: Make a release

65.breadcrumbs: Scope and fidelity to Phoebus » Scope and fidelity to Phoebus
65.title: Scope and fidelity to Phoebus

66.body: bobview is a viewer . It opens Phoebus Display Builder .bob screens and CS-Studio BOY .opi screens and shows live EPICS values on them, from a single small binary that starts quickly and runs on modest hardware: down to a phone, in the Android 16 Linux Terminal (Debian 13, aarch64). The same code builds for the browser.
66.breadcrumbs: Scope and fidelity to Phoebus » What bobview is for
66.title: What bobview is for

67.body: Scripts (Jython and JavaScript) are not run. The status line shows "N widgets with scripts ignored", counting widgets, not scripts. A few scripts that are common in DLS and techui-builder screens are recognised by name and done natively instead; see How BOY screens are translated and Widgets . Display editing. Use Phoebus to edit screens. Alarm and archiver services. Trends are live only, with no archived history. Widgets bobview can't draw are shown as a grey placeholder labelled with the widget type and PV name, and the status line counts "N unsupported widgets". What is and isn't supported is listed in Widgets .
67.breadcrumbs: Scope and fidelity to Phoebus » What is out of scope
67.title: What is out of scope

68.body: Fidelity is approximate. Sizes, fonts (scaled by 0.95) and layout were tuned by eye, and output has not been compared with Phoebus's own pixel for pixel. Where behaviour matters more than looks, bobview follows Phoebus closely: number formats, how typed text is parsed into a value (units dropped, 0x and 0b numbers, enum labels), macro expansion, and the precedence of operators in rules (as Phoebus's Jython for a .bob, as BOY's JavaScript for an .opi). Where it departs from Phoebus it says so in the reference, for example rules taking the integer part of a double for bitwise operators where Jython would fail.
68.breadcrumbs: Scope and fidelity to Phoebus » How close it is to Phoebus
68.title: How close it is to Phoebus

69.body: Channel Access and PV Access come from the third-party epics-rs crates, which are young; see Architecture . So far bobview has mainly been exercised against the in-repo bobview-testioc, not a real softIOC, PVXS or ca-gateway. The interop CI job and crates/pv/tests/interop.rs are there to change that.
69.breadcrumbs: Scope and fidelity to Phoebus » Protocol maturity
69.title: Protocol maturity

7.body: From the home display, open the ea-test display. Type a new number into the text entry for bl01t:A and press Enter, or drag its slider. bl01t:SUM follows, as the calculator record adds A and B.
7.title: 6. Change a value

70.body: bobview is a Cargo workspace of five crates: crate what bob the display model: reads .bob files and translates .opi ones into the same form, expands macros, resolves Eclipse project links and DLS launchers pv PV connections behind one interface: Channel Access, PV Access, PVWS for the browser, loc://, sim:// and formula PVs bobview the viewer: an egui app that draws displays, plus bobview-probe bobview-server serves the web build, .bob files and a PV Web Socket from one port testioc bobview-testioc, a pure-Rust IOC serving the example-services BL01T PVs
70.title: Architecture

71.body: bob reads a display, from a file or over http(s), into a tree of widgets with their properties. An .opi is translated as it is read, so everything after this step sees only the .bob form. Macros are expanded down the tree; rules are kept as expressions over the PVs they read. bobview connects each widget's PVs through pv and draws the tree with egui every frame, re-evaluating rules as values arrive.
71.title: From file to screen

72.body: pv's ca.rs and pva.rs are thin adapters over the epics-rs epics-ca-rs and epics-pva-rs crates, which do the protocol work. These are young, so protocol correctness rests largely on them; the interop CI job tests against other EPICS implementations.
72.title: Protocols

73.body: The pv and bobview crates also build for wasm32-unknown-unknown, drawn with WebGL. A browser can't speak CA or PVA, so there PVs come over a PV Web Socket (PVWS), as in Daedalus. bobview-server provides one at /pvws/pv, reaching PVs through the same pv crate as the desktop viewer; any other PVWS server works too. loc:// and sim:// PVs are made in the page itself.
73.title: In the browser

74.body: bobview-testioc serves enough of the epics-containers example-services BL01T beamline for its screens, over CA and PVA, with no C dependencies. It runs natively on an aarch64 phone, where the real amd64 IOC containers would need qemu, and CI uses it to snapshot every test display. See bobview-testioc .
74.title: The test IOC

75.body: For a control room, several displays can be open side by side, each in a window of its own, and the arrangement saved as a layout . The question is where a link opens its display: in place, or in another window? bobview answers it with one idea: each window is pinned or not.
75.breadcrumbs: Pinned windows and the viewer » Pinned windows and the viewer
75.title: Pinned windows and the viewer

76.body: A link (an action or menu button, a symbol click …) opens its display by these rules, whatever target the screen gives it: Click Display already open somewhere Not open in a pinned window raise that window open in the viewer, or a new window if every window is pinned in an unpinned window raise that window open in place shift +click raise that window open in a new window ctrl +click open in place open in place The viewer is the unpinned window used last (focused, opened or unpinned), so clicking a window once makes it where the next link goes. "Already open" means the same display with the same macros, in another window.
76.breadcrumbs: Pinned windows and the viewer » The rule
76.title: The rule

77.body: The main window starts pinned, so it stays where it is while the displays it links to come and go in one other window: an overview on one side and a detail on the other. Pin that one too to keep it, and the next link opens a new viewer. Unpinned, the main window navigates in place, as a single window does. Holding shift opens every display in a window of its own, as the old multi-window mode did. A display opened in place or in the viewer keeps that window's history for Back and Forward. A link to the display its own window shows reloads it in place, as a Refresh button wants, without adding to Back. BOY Exit buttons close the display window they are in (in the main window they go back). In a browser, and on a touch or small screen, displays have no windows of their own: every link navigates in place, and the pin and layout controls are not shown.
77.breadcrumbs: Pinned windows and the viewer » Why it works this way
77.title: Why it works this way

78.body: A display window opens sized to its display at 100%, within the monitor, beside the window pinned last, so a row of small windows grows beside a big one: on the first of its right, below it, its left and above it where there is room on the monitor clear of the pinned windows. Failing that it goes beside the window whose link opened it, then beside the other pinned windows, or where it covers them least. The viewer is sized and placed so again for each display a pinned window's link opens in it. Wayland doesn't let applications place their windows, so there the compositor does.
78.breadcrumbs: Pinned windows and the viewer » Where new windows go
78.title: Where new windows go

79.body: Each window is redrawn on its own: for its own input, and when a PV its display shows changes (at most 10 times a second), not when another window is. That matters most over ssh -X, where each redraw sends the whole window over the network. The controls of each window are listed in The window and its controls .
79.breadcrumbs: Pinned windows and the viewer » Redrawing
79.title: Redrawing

8.body: Close the window to quit bobview, then stop the IOC: kill %1
8.title: 7. Finish

80.breadcrumbs: How BOY screens are translated » How BOY screens are translated
80.title: How BOY screens are translated

81.body: An .opi file (CS-Studio BOY) is translated as it is read into the .bob form, the way Phoebus's own legacy import converts it, so it is drawn by the same widgets as a .bob. It is accepted everywhere a .bob is: on the command line, in Open… (which lists .opi files too), in actions and linking containers, and over http(s). As in Phoebus, a .bob next to a named .opi file is opened in its place. How each BOY widget is drawn is listed in BOY widgets .
81.breadcrumbs: How BOY screens are translated » One renderer for both formats
81.title: One renderer for both formats

82.body: Colours keep the RGB the file gives; a colour with only a name is looked up in the EDM colors.list DLS converted its screens with, then in the Phoebus palette. Fonts in pixels keep their size, fonts in points are divided by 1.01, and the Phoebus named fonts (Default, Header 1 …) use the Phoebus sizes. Rules keep BOY's severity numbers (pvSev0 becomes pvLegacySev0) and widget.getValue() reads the widget's own PV.
82.breadcrumbs: How BOY screens are translated » Colours, fonts and rules
82.title: Colours, fonts and rules

83.body: An .opi keeps its declared width and height, and widgets outside them are clipped, as in BOY. EDM conversions often leave stray widgets far off the display, which Phoebus (and bobview, for a .bob) would grow the display to show. This size is also what Fit, --size auto and an embedding container that sizes itself to its content use.
83.breadcrumbs: How BOY screens are translated » Size and clipping
83.title: Size and clipping

84.body: Scripts and JavaScript or Python actions are not run, with these exceptions, recognised and done by bobview itself: The EDM Exit button's script (ScriptUtil.closeAssociatedOPI) goes back to the previous display, or closes the window. A script that opens a Data Browser on some PVs (ScriptUtil.executeEclipseCommand of org.csstudio.trends.databrowser2.newWindow with ['pvnames', 'A,B'], as the DLS vacuum "Graph" buttons do) opens a trend of them. The DLS vacuum widget script get_pv_name.py, recognised by its file name. Its second PV, a vacuum space's link field such as SR03S-VA-SPACE-01:IONPSTA.INPA, names a group (SR03S-VA-GIONP-01:STA NPP NMS names SR03S-VA-GIONP-01). Each time it names a different one, a label shows the group's name, and any other widget reads the group's :STA and takes its name, so its tooltip, right-click menu and the $(name) its click passes as device follow. An EDM symbol of a gauge, ion pump or valve strip shows the frame for that status (0 when disconnected). A click on a shape, symbol or LED with a BOY click hook runs its actions. A disconnected EDM symbol shows its first frame inside the disconnected border, without Phoebus' overlay.
84.breadcrumbs: How BOY screens are translated » Scripts that are done natively
84.title: Scripts that are done natively

85.body: BOY screens name each other through the CS-Studio workspace: an Eclipse project whose .project links folder names to the directories that hold each module's screens. bobview resolves these links itself. DLS modules have no .project on disk, but the generated launcher runcss.sh beside a module's screens lists the links it gives CS-Studio (links="${SCRIPT_DIR}=${project}/${module},…"). bobview reads that list (it does not run the script, which needs configure-ioc), taking version from the module's configure/VERSION (else dev). So …/vacuum/4-100/vacuumApp/opi/opi/diamondVacuumOverview.opi opens as …/vacuumApp/opi/opi/runcss.sh/vacuum_4-100/vacuum/diamondVacuumOverview.opi: the CS-Studio path /vacuum_4-100/vacuum/diamondVacuumOverview.opi below the launcher, and links to other modules work. This is for BOY screens only: a .bob (even one Phoebus-style in place of an .opi, or one picked in a launcher project's folder) goes by its real path. A .project nearer the screen than the launcher, or beside it, wins when it links the screen (an empty one, as many DLS modules have, does not). The steps to open such screens are in Open BOY screens from an Eclipse project or DLS module .
85.breadcrumbs: How BOY screens are translated » Eclipse projects and DLS launchers
85.title: Eclipse projects and DLS launchers

86.body: DLS screens open others with command actions that run a launcher script, such as ./srCellVacuum 04, which ends by running runcss.sh DISPLAY -m MACROS to start CS-Studio. For a local display, bobview runs a copy of such a script beside a stand-in runcss.sh that only records its arguments, and opens that display with those macros. A command that starts StripTool (strip.py, strip.sh or buildStripToolconfig.sh and the PV names, as in the DLS vacuum, gauge and RGA screens) opens a trend of those PVs instead; a last word without a :, such as log_mbar, is ignored. Other commands are not run. Running scripts is limited for safety; see Writes and safety .
86.breadcrumbs: How BOY screens are translated » Launcher commands
86.title: Launcher commands

87.body: A viewer that can write to a control system needs to be predictable about when it does. This page explains the rules.
87.breadcrumbs: Writes and safety » Writes and safety
87.title: Writes and safety

88.body: --read-only refuses every write to a PV: controls are disabled and a write action says in the status line why it did nothing. loc:// PVs are exempt, as they live inside bobview and can't reach a control system.
88.title: Read-only mode

89.body: Channel Access reports whether a PV is writable, and controls follow it. PV Access does not report access rights, so such a PV is assumed writable (the PV details say "unknown"), and a put the server refuses is shown as a write error in the status line and the PV details.
89.title: Access rights

9.body: Point bobview at your own IOCs: Connect to real IOCs . Open your own screens: bobview path/to/screen.bob -m P=BL01T,R=:DET:. Show the same displays in a web browser: Serve displays to a browser .
9.title: Next steps

90.body: A write to a CA or PVA PV that was connected and has dropped is refused at once, rather than queued and applied when it comes back, possibly much later; the status line says so. So is a write while 16 earlier writes to the same PV still wait. A write to a PV that has yet to connect (as a write_pv action to a PV not on the display makes) waits for it, up to 5 s over CA, without holding up the PV's other events. The writes behind it wait in that queue (so while it waits, a 17th is refused), and fail with it if it gives up.
90.breadcrumbs: Writes and safety » Writes are never applied late
90.title: Writes are never applied late

91.body: A write_pv action and the toggle script write at once, as in Phoebus, whether the display came from a local file or an http:// or https:// URL. To open displays without letting them write, use --read-only, which refuses every write.
91.breadcrumbs: Writes and safety » Displays from the web
91.title: Displays from the web

92.body: No command is ever run for a display fetched over http(s), nor in a command_directory on the web. Only a launcher script that resolves (after macros, .. and project links) to a local file beside or under the display, or in a linked folder of its Eclipse project, is run. Anything else, such as an absolute path elsewhere or a ../.. escape, is refused and logged, as is a script that any user may change (world-writable, or in a world-writable folder). Each script run is logged.
92.title: Commands

93.body: bobview-server writes as its own user, so it allows writes only with --write, and each write must carry a token. A page with a token loads displays only from its own server, and sends the token only to a PVWS on its own server, so a link naming someone else's display or &pvws= cannot write with it. The page removes the token from its address after reading it. Writes to a PV that was connected and has dropped fail at once, and at most 16 may wait for one PV, as on the desktop. One to a PV that has yet to connect fails after 5 s, which the page sees only as the PV's write error, not as a message.
93.breadcrumbs: Writes and safety » In the browser
93.title: In the browser

95.body: bobview [OPTIONS] [DISPLAY] DISPLAY is a .bob or .opi file, or an http:// or https:// URL. With no display, bobview restores the default window layout when one has been saved, else opens index.bob from the bundled displays (~/.local/share/bobview/displays) when present, else a file chooser. option meaning -m, --macros P=X,R=Y macros for the display -p, --project DIR open the display through the linked folders of the Eclipse project in DIR (its .project, or for a BOY .opi screen the links of a DLS runcss.sh in DIR); see Open BOY screens -z, --zoom FACTOR fixed zoom, 0.2 to 5, instead of fitting the window -f, --fullscreen start full screen --read-only refuse every write to a PV except loc:// ones; see Writes and safety --layout NAME restore the saved layout NAME --no-layout don't restore the default layout --ui-scale F or auto size of the toolbar and menus relative to the desktop's scale, 1 being the desktop's own (default auto: smaller on a small high-DPI screen) --snapshot OUT.png render to a PNG without a window and exit; see Take snapshots --size WxH or auto snapshot size in pixels (default 1280x800); auto sizes it as a window manager would, on a 1920x1080 monitor --scale-factor F snapshot as on a screen with this desktop scale, e.g. 2.75 for a phone (default 1) --wait SECONDS time for PVs to connect before a snapshot (default 2) --click X,Y click here before the snapshot (repeatable) --right-click X,Y right-click here before the snapshot (repeatable) --settle SECONDS time after the last click before the snapshot (default 1) -h, --help show help -V, --version show the version
95.title: bobview

96.body: bobview-ssh [OPTIONS] [DISPLAY] Runs bobview with the same arguments, rendering with Mesa in software. See Choose bobview or bobview-ssh .
96.title: bobview-ssh

97.body: bobview-probe [--seconds N] [--put NAME=VALUE]... NAME... Prints live values of PVs through bobview's PV layer, for N seconds (default 5). --put writes a value first (repeatable). PV names take the same prefixes as in a display (pva://, loc:// …).
97.title: bobview-probe

98.body: bobview-server [OPTIONS] Serves the bobview web build, .bob files and a PV Web Socket on one port. Open http://HOST:PORT/?display=FILE.bob in a browser (default index.bob). See Deploy bobview-server for others . option meaning -p, --port PORT port to listen on (default 8080) --bind ADDR address to listen on (default 127.0.0.1, this machine only; 0.0.0.0 is every interface) --web DIR the web build from scripts/build-web.sh (default ../share/bobview/web next to this binary, else dist/web) --opi DIR serve .bob files from here; they take precedence over files of the same name in the web build --follow-symlinks serve files through symbolic links that lead out of --opi or --web (refused by default) --write let browsers write to PVs (off by default, as in PVWS); every write must carry the write token --write-token TOKEN the token --write wants (default: $BOBVIEW_WRITE_TOKEN if set and not empty, else a random one printed at startup); prefer the variable, as arguments show in ps --allow-origin ORIGIN also let pages from ORIGIN connect, e.g. https://host.example.com (repeatable) --host NAME let browsers call this server NAME, as well as an IP address, localhost, this machine's name and the hosts of --allow-origin (repeatable) --max-per-ip N most clients at once from one address (default 10) --throttle-ms MS least time between two batches of updates to one client (default 100) -h, --help show help -V, --version show the version
98.title: bobview-server

99.body: bobview-testioc [--only ea|motor|cam]... Serves the simulated BL01T PVs; by default all three parts. See bobview-testioc .
99.title: bobview-testioc
